title: A T. rex Tooth Stuck in a Skull Tells a 66-Million-Year-Old Story!
summary:
Imagine finding a fossil that's like a snapshot of a real dinosaur attack! That's exactly what scientists have at the Museum of the Rockies in Montana. It's a skull from a plant-eating dinosaur called Edmontosaurus, and it has a broken T. rex tooth still jammed in its face. How cool—and scary—is that?

This fossil is about 66 million years old. Back then, Tyrannosaurus rex was the top predator, and Edmontosaurus was a duck-billed giant that it might have hunted. The skull was dug up in 2005 in eastern Montana, but researchers just finished a detailed study. They used CT scans (like super-powered X-rays) to look inside the bone and figure out what happened.

Here's what they think: the T. rex bit the Edmontosaurus right on the nose, face-to-face. The tooth broke off and got stuck because the bite was so incredibly strong. There are no signs of healing on the bone, which means the Edmontosaurus either died from the bite or was already dead when the T. rex took a chomp. "The amount of force necessary for a tooth to have become broken off in bone points to the use of deadly force," said researcher Taia Wyenberg-Henzler. "For me, this paints a terrifying picture of the last moments of this Edmontosaurus."

Finding a tooth still stuck in a bone is super rare. Usually, scientists only find bite marks. But this tooth tells them exactly who did the biting—it matched T. rex teeth perfectly. It's like being a dinosaur detective, solving a case from millions of years ago. This discovery helps us understand how T. rex hunted and ate, adding one more piece to the puzzle of the most famous dinosaur ever.
why_it_matters: This tooth in a skull is like a detective clue that shows how dinosaurs really lived and hunted, sparking excitement about the past and the scientists who study it.

keywords.explanation: Edmontosaurus is a large, plant-eating dinosaur that had a wide, flat beak and lived 66 million years ago.
A fossil is the preserved remains, like bones or teeth, of an ancient animal or plant that have turned into stone.
CT scans are a medical imaging method that uses X-rays from many angles to create 3D pictures of the inside of something.
The Museum of the Rockies is a big museum in Montana famous for having many dinosaur skeletons and fossils.
Duck-billed means having a mouth shaped like a duck’s bill, which helped this dinosaur snip and chew tough plants.
A predator is an animal that hunts and kills other animals for food.

background_read: Edmontosaurus was one of the last large duck-billed dinosaurs, living in western North America around the same time as T. rex.
The Museum of the Rockies in Bozeman, Montana, holds one of the biggest collections of dinosaur fossils in the world, including many T. rex specimens.
Finding a predator’s tooth stuck in a prey’s bone is very rare and gives direct evidence of how ancient animals interacted.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at the Museum of the Rockies, led by researcher Taia Wyenberg-Henzler.
WHAT: Studying a 66-million-year-old Edmontosaurus skull with a broken T. rex tooth still stuck in the bone.
WHERE: The fossil was discovered in eastern Montana and is now at the museum.
WHY: To learn how Tyrannosaurus rex attacked and ate, and to get a rare glimpse of a dinosaur’s final moments.

perspectives.description: Paleontologists are thrilled because a tooth stuck in bone provides rare, direct evidence of predator-prey behavior, bringing the dinosaur world to life.
Budget-minded critics might say that studying old bones doesn’t address today’s environmental or social challenges.
Researchers see this as one important piece in a big puzzle; many more fossils are needed to fully understand T. rex’s hunting habits.
